title: Yajnavalkya's two words
hookLine: a king offers a thousand cows to the wisest sage, and the winner gives the self no label
carry: neti neti: you are the one who sees
last: DASYA AND VATSALYA: GOD AS KING, GOD AS CHILD.

lines: A THOUSAND COWS, GOLD ON THEIR HORNS.
cards: King Janaka wants to know who is the wisest sage in the land. So he pens up a thousand cows and ties gold to their horns. The wisest of you, he tells the gathered sages, may drive them home.
Nobody moves. Then Yajnavalkya calls to his student: drive them home. The hall erupts.
You think you're the wisest? Yajnavalkya shrugs. I bow to the wisest.
I just want the cows. So, one by one, the sages line up to test him. The last one keeps pushing: then describe the self.

teach.h: NETI, NETI: NOT THIS, NOT THIS.
teach.b: Neti, neti. Not this, not this. The story is in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, one of the oldest, and those two words are a classic doorway into the third path of yoga: jnana.

teach.h: JNA: TO KNOW, FROM THE INSIDE.
teach.b: Jnana comes from the Sanskrit root jna, to know, a cousin of the English word know and the Greek gnosis. But jnana doesn't mean information. You can't look it up.
It means knowing the way you know you're awake: direct, from the inside. Karma yoga asked what you do. Bhakti asked who you love.
Jnana asks who is doing and loving in the first place. So why won't Yajnavalkya give the self a label? Because whatever you can point at is not it.
Not the body. Not the breath. Not the thoughts, not the feelings.
Anything you can observe is something you're observing, so it can't be the observer.
Elsewhere in the same Upanishad he asks: by what would one know the knower? Your eye can see everything except itself.

This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings, especially in Vedanta: the atman, your real self, isn't the body or the mind but the awareness that knows them. So the jnana path works by subtraction, not addition.
And here's where it meets your life.

teach.h: YOU ARE THE ONE WHO SEES.
teach.b: Someone at a party asks, so, what do you do? You give a job, a city, a school, a family. Every one is true, and every one can be pointed at.
Neti, neti: not wrong, just not the whole of you. This week: a riverbank, a wife who turns down a fortune, and a boy bent in eight places.

how: In Vedanta, jnana yoga is practiced by studying the Upanishads with a teacher, reflecting on them, and meditating on the self as the witness of body and mind; 'not this, not this' (neti neti) is one of its classic tools.

s: jnana yoga means collecting as much information as possible
jnana is direct knowing of the self; the path works by subtraction, not addition.
Yajnavalkya turned down King Janaka's cows to show he was humble
he told his student to drive them home, then answered every sage who challenged him.
neti neti is a phrase from the Upanishads
Yajnavalkya uses it in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad to describe the self.

games.q: you ask Yajnavalkya to describe the real self, the true I. what does he say?
o: it's your soul, shaped like your body.
it's your mind at its best.
games.why: neti, neti. anything that can be pointed to is something known, so it isn't the knower.

practice: Notice the weight of your body on the seat and say inwardly, not this; then the breath, not this; then a thought passing through, not this, either.
Don't push anything away; just notice it's being noticed, and rest as the one noticing, without trying to describe it. If it slips away, begin again.

wordCard.voice: Jnana yoga. The path of knowledge: not information, but knowing from the inside who you are. Its first tool is neti, neti, not this, not this.

orig.note: Sanskrit: na iti, na iti, 'not so, not so' — Yajnavalkya's words in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad.

carryVoice: Your line: neti neti, you are the one who sees. Every label you can point at is not quite it. Day two seventy-four.
